question: Can the growth of a classifier's norm under gradient-based training explain power-law learning curves throughout training and recover the familiar data-scaling law at the best stopping point?

key_findings.claim: A fixed-norm teacher-student perceptron qualitatively tracks the free-norm gradient-descent trajectory and interpolates among Hebbian, Bayes-optimal, and maximum-stability regimes.
key_findings.evidence: For logistic loss at several sample-to-dimension ratios, the analytical fixed-norm error curves closely follow numerical free-norm trajectories when the constraint parameter is matched to the evolving weight norm. Small norm resembles the Hebb rule, an intermediate norm reaches the Bayes-optimal error, and unbounded norm approaches the maximum-margin solution and can overfit.

key_findings.claim: Two dynamical power laws compose into an end-of-training data scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: Before an elbow, normalized error decays as a power of norm, while the error-minimizing norm grows as a power of sample ratio. Rescaling both axes by the optimum collapses curves across data sizes; substituting the second relation into the first predicts that the final data exponent is the product of the two dynamical exponents.

key_findings.claim: The perceptron calculation yields the expected one-half data exponent with both analytical and trained dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: The fixed-norm solution has a norm-error exponent of one-half and an optimal-norm exponent of one; the free-norm fit reports 0.4901 plus or minus 0.0005 and 0.96 plus or minus 0.25, respectively, consistent with a product near one-half.

key_findings.claim: The exponent-product relation is empirically accurate across nine fixed-size vision architecture-dataset combinations when training progress is parameterized by spectral complexity.
key_findings.evidence: CNNs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 show approximate curve collapse. Table 1 reports predicted versus directly measured data exponents that agree within uncertainty, including 0.60 versus 0.55 for CNN-MNIST, 0.28 versus 0.25 for CNN-CIFAR-10, and 0.14 versus 0.12 for ViT-CIFAR-100.

key_findings.claim: The qualitative collapse is more robust than the specific quantitative norm explanation.
key_findings.evidence: Moderate weight decay and SGD change the two component exponents while preserving their product relation, but alternative L1, L2, group, and simple spectral norms often yield visually plausible collapse without accurately predicting the terminal data exponent. Mean-squared-error perceptron training is a counterexample, and plotting against epochs does not reproduce the norm collapse.

method.core_idea: Use model complexity, measured by a norm that grows along optimization, as the clock for learning dynamics; fit a power law from error to norm and another from optimal norm to dataset size, then multiply their exponents to predict end-of-training data scaling.
method.mechanism: The paper first solves a high-dimensional teacher-student perceptron with a fixed logistic-loss sharpness/norm constraint and compares it with free-norm gradient descent. It then trains fixed-size CNN, ResNet, and ViT classifiers over multiple dataset sizes and records test error against a Bartlett-style spectral complexity measure: the product of layer spectral norms times a sum of normalized deviations from reference weights. Per-dataset elbows give optimal norms and errors; log-log fits estimate the two dynamical exponents and their product.
assumptions: The chosen norm is a meaningful monotone coordinate for optimization progress and model complexity.
Learning curves contain a sufficiently wide pre-elbow power-law regime and a well-defined error-minimizing norm.
The teacher-student large-dimension limit captures mechanisms relevant to finite deep image classifiers.
Architecture, optimizer, and data distribution remain fixed while only sample count and training progress vary.
The two fitted scaling relations extrapolate to the same regime in which terminal data scaling is measured.

techniques.role: Analytically predicts perceptron overlap and generalization error at a prescribed norm in the high-dimensional teacher-student limit.
Replaces epochs with an evolving complexity coordinate to align trajectories across dataset sizes.
Extends the perceptron norm picture to deep networks using a product-of-spectral-norms margin-bound quantity.
Normalizes each curve by its minimum-error norm and error to expose a common master curve.
Multiplies the error-versus-norm and optimal-norm-versus-data exponents to predict the usual data-scaling exponent.

evaluations.setting: High-dimensional teacher-student perceptron with Rademacher inputs and logistic loss
evaluations.metric: Generalization error versus normalized weight norm over several sample ratios
evaluations.result: Fixed-norm analytical solutions qualitatively trace free-norm gradient descent and collapse after optimal-point rescaling
evaluations.baseline: Hebbian, Bayes-optimal, and maximum-stability classical learning rules

evaluations.setting: CNN, ResNet, and Vision Transformer on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100
evaluations.metric: Predicted product exponent versus directly fitted terminal test-error data exponent
evaluations.result: All nine reported pairs agree within quoted uncertainty; point estimates range from 0.14/0.12 to 0.60/0.55
SGD and moderate weight decay preserve the proposed relation while changing component exponents

evaluations.metric: Qualitative collapse and quantitative terminal-exponent prediction
evaluations.result: Several norms collapse curves qualitatively, but many give inaccurate exponent products

evaluations.setting: Perceptron with mean-squared-error loss and epoch-based plots
evaluations.result: The expected norm scaling is absent for MSE, and epochs do not substitute for norm as a collapsing coordinate

limitations: Deep-network evidence is restricted to small image-classification benchmarks and fixed model sizes; it does not test language models, generative objectives, or simultaneous width/depth scaling.
The fixed-norm equivalence is analytical only for a perceptron and merely qualitative for nonconvex deep networks.
The spectral complexity norm is selected because its exponent product works best; alternative plausible norms weaken the quantitative claim and create a model-selection risk.
Some component exponents are extreme or imprecise, such as very small ViT error-norm exponents paired with optimal-norm exponents near 18-21, so agreement of the product can mask unstable factors.
Power-law ranges span limited dataset and complexity scales, with no held-out large-scale extrapolation test.
Early stopping is defined using test-error minima, which is unavailable in deployment and can leak evaluation information unless a validation set is separated.
The MSE counterexample shows that the claimed mechanism is loss- and implicit-bias-dependent rather than universal.
failure_modes: A norm can increase monotonically without tracking function-space complexity, producing a visually clean but causally misleading collapse.
Selecting a complexity measure after inspecting exponent agreement can overfit the reported scaling relation.
Small errors in either component exponent become large relative errors when one exponent is near zero and the other is very large.
A distribution shift, architecture change, or optimizer phase transition can move the elbow and invalidate the master curve.
Training beyond the finite-data optimum can enter maximum-margin overfitting, so lower training loss and larger norm need not mean better generalization.
A small-scale fit may preserve the exponent product locally yet fail when larger models learn qualitatively new features.
reusable_insights: Parameterize learning curves by a measured state variable, not only wall-clock steps, when optimization speed varies across dataset sizes.
Decompose a terminal scaling law into a within-run improvement law and a resource-dependent stopping law; each component can reveal distinct interventions.
Require candidate complexity measures to forecast held-out scales rather than judging them only by retrospective curve collapse.
Report component exponents and their covariance, because agreement of their product alone can hide poorly identified mechanisms.
Use loss-function counterexamples to delimit when an implicit-bias explanation should apply.
open_questions: Does the exponent-product law predict held-out larger datasets and models before their training curves are observed?
Which function-space or representation-space complexity coordinate works across architectures without post-hoc norm selection?
Can a deep-network theory justify equivalence between an unconstrained trajectory and constrained minimizers at matched complexity?
How do data noise, nonseparability, label smoothing, augmentation, and modern regularization alter the elbow and implicit-bias regimes?
Can a validation-only stopping protocol retain the claimed scaling without using test error to choose the optimum?
Do analogous decompositions hold for language-model cross-entropy, reinforcement-learning returns, or generative likelihoods?

competitive_landscape.title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Establishes that unregularized gradient descent on separable logistic classification diverges in norm while converging in direction to the hard-margin solution.
competitive_landscape.difference: It characterizes the asymptotic implicit bias; the reviewed paper uses norm growth across the full trajectory to explain learning-curve scaling and finite-time overfitting.

competitive_landscape.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Derives training-time, data-size, and model-size scaling behavior in a solvable random-feature model.
competitive_landscape.difference: It attributes scaling to spectral learning dynamics and compute allocation; the reviewed paper centers an evolving norm and composes two norm-based exponents.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamical Decoupling of Generalization and Overfitting in Large Two-Layer Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses dynamical mean-field theory to connect slow growth of complexity with feature learning, overfitting, and non-monotone test error.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides a two-layer asymptotic dynamics with distinct time scales; the reviewed paper proposes a simpler cross-architecture empirical scaling coordinate and exponent composition.

competitive_landscape.title: Benefits of Early Stopping in Gradient Descent for Overparameterized Logistic Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Analyzes the whole overparameterized logistic-regression trajectory and relates early-stopped iterates to explicit L2 regularization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It proves statistical benefits and nonasymptotic comparisons in a specific regime; the reviewed paper seeks power-law regularities from norm growth across perceptrons and deep vision models.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
competitive_landscape.relationship: Documents empirical power-law generalization trends across data, model, and compute scales in multiple domains.
competitive_landscape.difference: It treats scaling largely as a terminal empirical regularity; the reviewed paper attempts to derive the data exponent from two within-training norm laws.

competitive_landscape.title: A Constructive Prediction of the Generalization Error Across Scales
competitive_landscape.relationship: Builds predictive functional forms for generalization error across sample and model scales.
competitive_landscape.difference: It forecasts terminal performance directly from scale variables; the reviewed paper decomposes terminal data scaling through a dynamical complexity coordinate.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims two new norm-based dynamical scaling laws whose exponent product recovers the standard end-of-training data scaling law, with an implicit-bias explanation from perceptrons to deep networks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A solvable logistic perceptron supplies the fixed-versus-free norm correspondence and analytical exponents; nine vision architecture-dataset pairs, optimizer/regularization variants, alternative norms, and counterexamples test the empirical pattern.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The clearest novelty is the particular two-law decomposition and optimal-point curve collapse. Training-time scaling, norm-driven implicit bias, and finite-time generalization are active prior lines, and the deep-network evidence does not yet establish that the selected spectral norm is the causal or universal state variable.

reviewer_notes: Read all 27 extracted pages, including theory, nine architecture-dataset experiments, norm ablations, optimizer and weight-decay checks, MSE and epoch counterexamples, and appendices. Competing primary records were checked on JMLR and arXiv on 2026-08-23.
